query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A trace addition of Hf, optimized to promote preferential segregation at the inter-lamellar boundaries of eutectic high-entropy alloys, will form ultrafine coherent or semi‐coherent Hf‐rich phases at these interfaces. This interfacial reinforcement is predicted to delay microcrack initiation under room-temperature tensile loading, simultaneously improving both the tensile strength (by impeding dislocation motion) and ductility (by inhibiting crack propagation) compared to the unmodified lamellar-colony structure.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies and numerous internal boundaries prone to microcrack initiation during room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Introduce an optimized minor alloying addition (trace doping) of Hf into the alloy composition.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile deformation; dopant concentrations must be narrowly controlled to avoid excessive precipitate coarsening or the formation of deleterious secondary phases.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of ultrafine, coherent (or semi-coherent) Hf-rich interfacial phases at the inter-lamellar boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The trace Hf segregates to the lamellar interfaces during processing, enhancing local cohesion. The resulting fine interfacial phases act as barriers to both dislocation motion and microcrack initiation/propagation, thereby improving the overall load bearing and delaying failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified baseline, the Hf-doped alloy is expected to show an increase in both tensile strength and ductility at room temperature. Specifically, the improved interface cohesion should raise the threshold for microcrack nucleation and slow crack propagation.
generation.baseline: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with a dual-phase lamellar microstructure that, in its as-produced state, exhibits high strength but limited ductility due to microcrack initiation along numerous internal boundaries.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only within a narrow Hf concentration range; excessive Hf may lead to precipitate coarsening or phase instability, while too low a concentration may not produce sufficient interfacial strengthening.
generation.uncertainty: While prior studies in similar systems (e.g., duplex steels and related high-entropy alloy investigations) support the concept of interface segregation strengthening, the precise optimal Hf concentration and the quantitative magnitude of improvements are currently uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of eutectic high-entropy alloy samples with systematically varied trace Hf concentrations within and around the expected optimal window while keeping the overall lamellar microstructure unchanged. Process all samples under identical conditions to ensure comparability.
measurements: Room-temperature tensile testing to obtain tensile strength and elongation data.
Microstructural characterization (using TEM/SEM coupled with EDS) to verify Hf segregation at inter-lamellar boundaries and to detect any formation of coarse or deleterious secondary phases.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples with the optimized Hf concentration do not exhibit statistically significant enhancements in both tensile strength and ductility relative to the undoped alloy, or if the interfacial regions reveal coarse or brittle secondary phases rather than fine coherent Hf-rich features, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Dual-phase high-entropy alloys with excellent room temperature and high-temperature properties have been widely studied as potential high-temperature structural materials. However, interface weakening causes its high-temperature performance to decline at higher temperatures, severely limiting further development. In this study, a series of Al17Cr10Fe36Ni36Mo1Hfx (x = 0, 0.03, 0.15, 0.3, 0.5, and 0.8 at%) alloys were prepared to study the effect of Hf content on the microstructure and mechanical properties of the matrix alloy. The results indicate that with the addition of the Hf, the Hf-rich phase began to precipitate at the interface and inside the B2 phase in the matrix alloy. In contrast, the morphology of both the FCC and B2 phases had no noticeable change. With the increase in Hf content, the high-temperature strength and ductility of the alloy first increased and then decreased, while the room temperature performance remained almost unchanged. As we all know, the alloying of metals with certain specific elements can very effectively improve alloy properties through various strengthening methods such as precipitation strengthening, solution strengthening, and interface strengthening [,,,]. Hf is an essential alloying element for both the interface strengthening of superalloys and the strengthening of the Ni-Al B2 phase [,,,,,]. Recently, some studies have shown that adding a small amount of Hf to a single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy could improve the room-temperature mechanical property of the alloy without significantly reducing the ductility of the alloy through the precipitation of intermetallic compounds such as Ni7Hf2 and Laves phases [,]. However, these studies mainly focus on single-phase high-entropy alloys, and the addition of Hf is relatively large, usually more than one atom. Therefore, the effect of trace Hf addition on the properties of the alloy at room temperature and high temperature is worthy of in-depth investigation.

frame.system: Eutectic high‐entropy alloys in their as‐produced state that consist of dual-phase lamellar colonies with many internal boundaries.
frame.goal: To concurrently improve both the tensile strength and room‐temperature ductility by mitigating microcrack initiation at internal boundaries.
frame.limitation: Conventional processing approaches and a variety of microstructural-design strategies have yielded higher strength at the cost of ductility, and none have eliminated the room-temperature brittleness associated with microcrack initiation from the colony’s numerous internal boundaries.

constraints: The intervention must improve both strength and ductility simultaneously at room temperature
It should involve a single modification rather than a combination of strategies
The basic lamellar-colony microstructure is retained as the baseline state
prior_attempts: Conventional thermomechanical processing methods that increase strength but reduce ductility
Various microstructural-design and processing strategies attempted previously that failed to overcome intrinsic brittleness of the lamellar colonies
frame.understanding: The absence of an interfacial modification that both suppresses premature microcrack initiation at lamellar boundaries and simultaneously provides resistance to plastic instability is the key shortcoming; prior methods improved one property at the expense of the other.
frame.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled minor alloying addition (or trace doping) that preferentially segregates to the inter-lamellar boundaries will enhance the local cohesion at these interfaces. This segregation forms ultrafine, coherent or semi-coherent interfacial phases (or solute atmospheres) that inhibit microcrack nucleation without compromising, and potentially even enhancing, the load-bearing capacity of the primary lamellar phases. Relative to the unmodified baseline, the doped alloy is expected to exhibit both increased tensile strength (due to an improved obstacle to dislocation motion and enhanced boundary strength) and improved ductility (via delayed crack initiation and propagation). The hypothesis is valid provided that the dopant concentration is kept within a narrow window to avoid precipitate coarsening or phase instability. Prior evidence from duplex steels and certain high-entropy alloy studies has shown that interface segregation can improve both toughness and strength. An experiment to falsify this hypothesis would be to process and test a set of tensile samples with varying levels of the trace element; if at optimal concentration the samples do not exhibit a statistically significant enhancement in both strength and ductility compared to the baseline—or if detrimental secondary phases form that reduce overall mechanical performance—the hypothesis would be refuted.

families.principle: Altering the chemical composition can encourage desirable solute segregation that strengthens interfacial cohesion and modifies dislocation dynamics.

cues_against: none explicitly, though prior attempts with processing routes suggest chemical composition has not been the focus
families.best_lever: Introduce an optimized concentration of a trace element that segregates to inter-lamellar boundaries to form ultrafine, coherent secondary phases, thereby reinforcing the interfaces without altering the overall lamellar morphology.
